tagline: An anonymous sermon in letter form, urging weary Christians to hold on because Jesus is the final word of God and the great high priest.
overview:
Hebrews is the most sustained argument in the New Testament, and one of its most beautiful pieces of Greek. It begins without a greeting, like a sermon, and ends with personal news and greetings, like a letter. Its author calls it a word of exhortation (13:22). It was written to believers who had once suffered bravely for their faith but were now tired, drifting, and tempted to give up on Christ, most likely by turning back to the familiar world of the synagogue, its priesthood, and its sacrifices.

The author's answer is not simply to scold but to show them who Jesus is. Page after page, he compares Jesus with the greatest things in Israel's faith: the prophets, the angels through whom the law was given, Moses, Joshua, Aaron and the priesthood, the tabernacle, the covenant made at Sinai, and the sacrifices of the Day of Atonement. Each was good and God-given, and each was a shadow pointing ahead. Jesus is the Son through whom God has spoken last and best, a priest in the order of Melchizedek who offered himself once for all and now lives to intercede for his people.

Woven through the argument are five solemn warnings not to drift, harden, fall away, or refuse the one who speaks, and just as many words of encouragement. The book ends with its great roll call of faith (chapter 11), a call to run the race looking to Jesus (chapter 12), and practical instructions for life together (chapter 13). Few books so thoroughly connect the Old Testament to Christ, and few speak so directly to people who are tired of believing.
author:
The author never gives a name, and no one knows for certain who wrote Hebrews. The writer was a skilled Greek stylist, knew the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint, the translation made in Egypt in the centuries before Christ) intimately, was a second-generation believer who heard the gospel from those who had heard the Lord (2:3), and knew Timothy (13:23).

In the Greek-speaking East the letter was associated with Paul from an early date; the oldest surviving collection of Paul's letters, the papyrus known as P46 from around AD 200, places it right after Romans. Yet even there scholars noticed that its style differed from Paul's. Clement of Alexandria, as reported by the historian Eusebius, thought Paul wrote it in Hebrew and Luke translated it. Origen judged that the thoughts were Paul's but the wording someone else's, and concluded that only God knows who actually wrote it. In the West, Tertullian attributed it to Barnabas, a Levite (Acts 4:36) and Paul's companion, and the Latin churches were slow to accept it as Pauline or even as Scripture until the late fourth century. Martin Luther proposed Apollos, the eloquent Alexandrian Jew learned in the Scriptures (Acts 18:24). Adolf von Harnack in 1900 suggested Priscilla, which would explain the missing name. Others have proposed Luke, Silas, or Clement of Rome. Most scholars today, whatever their theology, take Origen's view: the author is unknown, and the letter's authority does not depend on the name.
date: Hebrews was known and used by Clement of Rome in the letter usually called 1 Clement, generally dated around AD 96, so it was written before then. Many scholars date it before AD 70, when the Romans destroyed the temple in Jerusalem. The author speaks of sacrifices in the present tense and argues that the old system is "aging" and will "soon disappear" (8:13); it would have been the strongest possible point to mention that the temple had already fallen, and he never does. Others date it in the 70s or 80s, noting that the author discusses the wilderness tabernacle rather than the Herodian temple, so the present tenses may be the vivid language of Scripture study rather than evidence that sacrifice was still being offered. The readers had suffered earlier but had not yet shed blood (10:32-34, 12:4), which some connect with the expulsion of Jews from Rome under the emperor Claudius around AD 49 and date the letter before Nero's persecution in AD 64. A date in the 60s is the most common view, with a range from about AD 60 to 90.
setting:
The title To the Hebrews is not part of the text, but it is very old and reflects what the letter itself suggests: readers steeped in the Scriptures and the institutions of Israel, for whom the priesthood and sacrifices were a live alternative. Most interpreters think of a community of Jewish Christians, perhaps with Gentile members as well, who were tempted to retreat into the synagogue, which Roman authorities generally tolerated as an ancestral religion in a way they did not tolerate the new movement. Some scholars argue for a mainly Gentile audience drawn to Jewish practice.

The location is unknown. The greeting from "those from Italy" (13:24) most naturally means Italians abroad sending greetings home, which suggests a church in or near Rome, and the letter's early use in Rome by Clement fits. Jerusalem, Alexandria, and other cities have been proposed. The readers had suffered public insult, imprisonment, and the confiscation of property in their early days (10:32-34), had endured it joyfully, and now faced discouragement and perhaps a new wave of pressure.
purpose: The author writes to keep a tired congregation from abandoning Christ. His method is to show that Jesus fulfills and surpasses everything they might go back to: he is the final revelation of God, the true high priest, the mediator of the new covenant promised in Jeremiah, and the one sacrifice that truly cleanses the conscience. Because this is so, turning back would mean turning away from the only real access to God. The letter alternates exposition (who Jesus is) with exhortation (so hold on, draw near, and encourage one another), and it ends by calling the readers to go out to Jesus "outside the camp" and bear his disgrace (13:13).
story: Hebrews reads the whole Old Testament as one story moving toward Christ. It takes up creation and rest (Genesis 1 and 2), Abraham and Melchizedek (Genesis 14), the exodus and the wilderness rebellion (Numbers 14 and Psalm 95), the tabernacle and the Day of Atonement (Exodus 25 to 40 and Leviticus 16), the royal psalms (Psalms 2, 45, and 110), and the prophetic promise of a new covenant (Jeremiah 31). It then shows the church standing where Israel stood in the wilderness, between redemption and the promised rest, hearing God's voice "Today". The story runs forward to the unshakable kingdom and the city that is to come (12:28, 13:14), the same city the last chapters of Revelation describe.
christ: No book of the New Testament has more to say about Christ's priesthood. Hebrews presents Jesus as the eternal Son through whom God made the universe (1:2), the exact representation of God's nature (1:3), and also fully human: made like his brothers in every way, tempted, crying out with tears, and learning obedience through suffering (2:17, 4:15, 5:7-8). Because he is both, he can be the perfect priest. He offered himself as the sacrifice, entered the true sanctuary in heaven with his own blood, sat down at God's right hand because the work was finished, and always lives to intercede (7:25). His one offering accomplishes what the repeated sacrifices never could, and he will appear a second time to bring salvation to those who wait for him (9:28).
reading: Hebrews is a sermon built on Old Testament texts. It helps to read it with those texts open, especially Psalms 2, 8, 95, 110, Genesis 14, Leviticus 16, and Jeremiah 31. The author often quotes the Septuagint, so his wording sometimes differs from English translations of the Hebrew. Watch for the pattern of argument from lesser to greater (if the old was binding, how much more the new), for the word better, which appears again and again, and for the constant alternation between teaching and warning. The warning passages (2:1-4, 3:7-4:13, 5:11-6:12, 10:26-39, 12:14-29) should be read together and in context; they are addressed to a congregation the author believes will persevere (6:9). A common misreading treats Hebrews as contempt for Judaism. The author honors the old covenant as God's own gift and argues that its purpose was to point to what has now come.

structure.title: The Son, greater than the angels
structure.summary: God has spoken finally in his Son, who is superior to the angels, yet the Son became human, lower than the angels for a while, to suffer, destroy death, and become a merciful high priest. The first warning urges the readers not to drift away.

structure.title: Greater than Moses: entering God's rest
structure.summary: Jesus is faithful as a Son over God's house, as Moses was as a servant in it. Psalm 95 and the wilderness generation warn the church not to harden its heart but to enter the Sabbath rest that still remains.

structure.title: A high priest in the order of Melchizedek
structure.summary: Jesus is a sympathetic high priest, appointed by God. After rebuking the readers' immaturity and warning of falling away, the author assures them of God's oath and shows that Melchizedek's priesthood, eternal and confirmed by oath, surpasses Aaron's.

structure.title: A better covenant, sanctuary, and sacrifice
structure.summary: Christ ministers in the true tabernacle as mediator of the new covenant promised in Jeremiah 31. The Day of Atonement pointed ahead to his single offering of himself, which cleanses the conscience and perfects believers once for all.

structure.title: Draw near and endure by faith
structure.summary: The readers are urged to draw near, hold fast, and meet together, warned against deliberate rejection, and reminded of their earlier courage. The heroes of faith and Jesus himself model endurance, and the unshakable kingdom calls for grateful worship.

structure.title: Life together and farewell
structure.summary: Practical instructions on love, hospitality, marriage, money, and leaders, a call to go to Jesus outside the camp, a benediction, and personal greetings.

themes.title: God has spoken in his Son
themes.body: The letter opens by contrasting God's many and partial words through the prophets with his final word in the Son. That word demands attention, and throughout the book the question is whether the readers will listen "Today" or harden their hearts. Scripture itself is presented as the living voice of God, often introduced with the words the Holy Spirit says.

themes.title: Jesus the great high priest
themes.body: Hebrews is the only New Testament book to call Jesus a priest explicitly and at length. He is appointed by God, like Aaron, but in the order of Melchizedek; he is able to sympathize because he was tempted; he offers not animals but himself; and he intercedes forever. The priesthood and sacrifices of Israel are the vocabulary through which the author explains the cross.

themes.title: Better things: fulfillment, not dismissal
themes.body: The word better runs through the book: a better hope, covenant, promises, sacrifices, possession, country, and resurrection. The old is called a copy and shadow, not because it was false, but because it pointed to a reality it could not itself provide. The new covenant fulfills the old rather than contradicting it.

themes.title: Perseverance and warning
themes.body: The readers are in danger of drifting, and the author warns them in the strongest terms that turning away from Christ leaves no other sacrifice for sin. Yet the same author is confident of better things in their case and grounds their hope in God's oath and Christ's intercession. How the warnings relate to assurance is one of the most debated questions in Christian theology.

themes.title: Faith as pilgrim endurance
themes.body: Faith in Hebrews looks forward. It trusts God's promise when the fulfillment is unseen, lives as a stranger and exile, and keeps going under pressure. The heroes of chapter 11 died without receiving what was promised, and Jesus, the founder and perfecter of faith, endured the cross for the joy set before him (12:2).

keyChapters.why: The majestic opening: God's final word in the Son, the radiance of his glory, who made purification for sins and sat down at God's right hand.
The Son shares our flesh and blood, tastes death for everyone, and becomes a merciful and faithful high priest.
The Sabbath rest that remains, the living word of God, and the invitation to approach the throne of grace with confidence.
The sharpest warning against falling away, followed by the anchor of hope secured by God's oath.
Melchizedek and the eternal priesthood of Jesus, who always lives to intercede.
The tabernacle and the Day of Atonement read as pointers to Christ's once-for-all sacrifice.
The great roll call of faith, from Abel to the unnamed martyrs.
Running the race with eyes fixed on Jesus, the discipline of the Father, and the unshakable kingdom.
